Preventing the next pandemic

By: Laura Byrne | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Most of us didn't see the COVID-19 pandemic coming. But scientists worldwide researching diseases with pandemic potential warn that this is not the last or the worst pandemic coming our way.

Unique Selling Point:
In the middle of the worst pandemic in a century, we speak to the scientists for whom pathogens like SARS-CoV-2 are bread and butter. We will visit Africa's only biosafety level 4 laboratory, at the NICD and get unique access to a cave in Limpopo where scientists from UP are monitoring infectious diseases circulating in local bat populations.

We ask: What do we know about emerging infectious diseases? How do we identify unknown threats? What are the driving factors of the increase in zoonotic spill-over events? How can we prevent another COVID-19?

Summary:
In 2018 the WHO added Disease X to its list of priority diseases for which to develop vaccines and treatments. Disease X would “have a mortality rate higher than a season flu but [one that] would spread as easily as the flu…. It would shake financial markets even before it achieved pandemic status.” Sound familiar?

The last few decades have seen an acceleration in outbreaks of known and new diseases. Zoonotic infections (diseases that 'spill over' from animals to humans) and especially viruses have been identified as a growing threat. 60% of human diseases come from animals and 75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic. There is a 'spill-over' event 1-2 times per year: an increase of 2-3 times what it was 40 years ago.

Around the world, virologists have been raising the red flag about the ways in which our overpopulated, environmentally compromised

Further information:
ZOONOTIC INFECTIONS
Zoonotic infectious diseases cause 2.5 billion illnesses and 2.7 million deaths/year. It’s estimated that there are 500 thousand unknown viruses with zoonotic potential. One project found more than 50 SARS-related viruses in bats. It could be so much worse than coronavirus – think about HIV which has killed 65 million people and doesn’t have a cure or a vaccine. Think about SARS with a 10% fatality rate. Or H7N9 with a 40% fatality rate. Or Ebola with 50%.

It takes three steps for a zoonotic agent to become pandemic:
1. a human must be exposed to the virus.
2. the virus must either be virulent or become so through mutation.
3. the virus must be able to move from human to human and not kill its host so quickly that it doesn't have time to spread.

Each presents opportunities to intervene, but traditionally, the study of infectious disease has focused on containing and tracing outbreaks after they’ve started.

CONTRIBUTING FACTORS:
Overpopulation
Travel and globalisation
Encroachment into wild habitats by humans and our farms.
Climate change
- Biodiversity loss: less dilution, more host-sharing.
- Increased interaction between species and with humans.
- Increased tick and mosquito-borne diseases.
- Shifting habitats, imbalances
Increased demand for animal food products (increased NCDs)
Bush meat trade (3.4 million tonnes in Africa every year alone)
Intensive agricultural practices, especially animal farming
- Genetically similar breeds in cramped, stressful, unsanitary conditions
- Humans increase contact between different animal species. Domestic animals share highest number of viruses with humans
- Land use change is the biggest predictor.
- Waste management and anti-microbial resistance: Incubating more virulent and drug resistant strains in domestic animals; 70% of antibiotics are used in farming.
- Livestock is 60% of mammal biomass (wildlife 4%). Poultry 70% of bird biomass. Raise and kill 75 billion animals/year.
Pandemic is going to worsen AMR: antibiotic prescription, sanitizers.

Strategies:
- Early detection, early response. Rapid diagnostics
- Universal vaccines and drugs
- Surveillance at the contact edge
- Food/agricultural and environmental interventions. The cost of COVID is around $5-15 trillion versus $22 billion to reduce deforestation and wildlife trafficking

CHALLENGES:
Wartime budgets are seen as unnecessary in peacetime. The US has reduced funding to programmes for emerging disease research under Trump. Fragmentation of global networks and growing populism threaten bodies like the WHO (it was the UN that funded and organised the drive to eradicate the only disease we have ever actually conquered: smallpox)
Science to policy is a big leap.
No coordinated response/uniform policy even within the US or EU.

Extra Budget Items:
1. Travel to Limpopo for two nights to film UP scientists at work monitoring bat populations. They will accommodate us in tents and have said they will cover the costs of our food and PPE
2. Vaccinations for all crew: tetanus and rabies. Tetanus is a once-off; rabies requires two doses 7 days apart. The second dose must be 28 days before the trip. Total cost approx R3 936.84
3. Extra shoot day with internal camera to film at the lab and interview NICD scientists in Joburg

Press Release:


Bat’s What We’re Talking About!
For decades, scientists have predicted a highly contagious pandemic would one day ravage the world’s population and crash global financial markets. They didn’t know how it would start, but they knew to follow the clues. Then the COVID-19 pandemic finally proved them right. Now, South African researchers are heading into bat caves in search of crucial scientific data that could help prevent the next pandemic.

Script:


CLAIRE TIKTOK VIDEOS: Nurse: Well done. What a well-behaved lady!
Claire: They gave me a lollipop!

LINK: Over a year ago, I was subjected to a very painful series of injections, all in the name of storytelling. Thanks to the pandemic, it’s taken some time to get here, but I’m about to meet a population of bats.

VO: I have a team of researchers patiently waiting to do the introductions. The colony roosts in a deep sinkhole. Dr Low de Vries gives me a quick rundown on what to expect…

UPSOUND: Low de Vries: Once you get inside it’s a bit small, so just watch your head…
Claire: Say nice things, Low. Say nice things…

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We choose specific sites where we think there's a risk of transmission in terms of the environment, livestock sometimes in the areas, or people. This specific site, we chose because it's in an urban area, so it's close to cities.

VO: For over a decade, Professor Wanda Markotter has tested bats for zoonotic pathogens: that is, diseases that commonly occur in animals, but may “spill over” into human beings.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We’re virologists, which means we're looking for viruses, but to get to the virus part, we need the samples. We go down, we catch the bats and we get the samples. And then we go into the lab where we identify the viruses.

VO: The first team has just emerged with a handful of bats – carefully transported in fabric bags. These are long-fingered bats, known to carry zoonotic diseases - which is why the researchers wear protective gear to handle them.

LINK: Sixty percent of human diseases come from animals, and 75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic. Some more familiar names: smallpox, ebola. HIV, and COVID-19.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: Unfortunately, the species that we identify the most viruses in are bats. They have large diversity, there's more than 1400 species. So that's one of the reasons why we're identifying a lot of viruses in them: there's a lot of bats.

VO: Besides taking blood, saliva and faecal samples for analysis in the lab, the scientists also tattoo each bat with a unique number so they can track individuals over time.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: And we're also looking at human behaviour. We're looking at the environment - if people have contact with the bats in this area. And then all that data are made available to the governmental departments so that they can do risk assessments.

VO: This batch of bats is returning to the cave, which means it’s time for me to suit up!

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: It’s about to get real, friends…

VO: This is serious PPE: overalls, a double layer of gloves and rubber boots.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Research chic!

VO: This space-age helmet with built-in respirator ensures that I won’t inhale the air inside the cave. Although the viruses lurking there may not be identical to those that infect humans, it’s vital that we don’t give them a chance to jump hosts.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: I’m ready, guys.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: It's all about adaptation. So if you look at the bat viruses, very few of them have the correct protein to bind to a human cell.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Wish me luck!

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: But let's say I go into this cave every day and I go and crawl around...You give those viruses the opportunity to see human cells every day, they start evolving. And the virus are going to change, to infect the new host.

UPSOUND: Camerawoman: What did he say?
Claire Mawisa: There's a rung missing at the bottom of the very rusty ladder!

VO: Unfazed by the flustered bats, our scientists get to work. Urine and faeces often harbour pathogens and are an easy route for disease transmission.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We take one swab to take a bit of faecal, we put it in a tube and that goes to the lab…

LINK: The proximity of this bat population to the urban human population is a big part of the problem. Rubbing shoulders with wildlife in habitats that used to be theirs means we’re not only sharing their space: we might also start sharing their diseases.

UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: Undoubtedly there is an increase in these spillover events. It's - there are many drivers. Most of them are what we call anthropogenic, which means they're based on humans. More and more we are putting pressure on wildlife and their habitats, including eating them, selling them, moving them around, keeping them as pets.

VO: Professor Delia Randolph is an epidemiologist whose research focuses on the role of food in novel disease outbreaks, especially the food sold in informal markets.

UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: You will see wild meat along with domestic meat, along live animals along with dead animals all mixed up. Food, which might be maybe even condemned in one place, gets diverted and sold in another place. So these foods are an opportunity of bringing people into contact with new diseases.

UPSOUND: Low de Vries: What we always do is we look for a tattoo number. So then we know she’s a recapture.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: This is gonna go for processing and come back.

VO: With that, visiting time is over…

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: I have so much respect for the scientists who do this work, but it’s time for me to get out of here!

VO: …and what goes down, must go up again.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Ah, not again!

LINK: In 2018, the WHO added an unknown Disease X to its list of priority diseases for which to develop vaccines and treatments. Disease X would have a mortality rate higher than that of the seasonal flu but would spread as easily as the flu. It would shake financial markets before it reached pandemic status. Sound familiar?

UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: Epidemiologists have been saying for decades there is going to be a big human pandemic, which is going to kill millions of people and cost trillions of dollars but no one believed us. If you pick up these new diseases just as they're spilling over, you can save more than 90 percent of the costs.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: You have to think differently after this pandemic. If I'm just going into a cave testing for pathogens, what difference are that going to make?

UPSOUND: Tedson Nkoana: We interact a lot with the kids because kids act as amplifiers of knowledge.

VO: This is where Markotter’s colleague Tedson Nkoana comes in, running community education sessions as part of a United Nations initiative to help curb the impact of COVID-19.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: what is the response? Do they get it?
Tedson Nkoana: I have to say I've gotten quite a positive response from the areas that we worked on, and people are now beginning to grasp the idea that there's these bats that might be carrying these diseases and we don't have to be scared of them.

VO: The sessions emphasise the risk of contact with points of disease transmission like urine or saliva. But Nkoana also seeks to change the narrative about bats.

UPSOUND: Tedson Nkoana: Bats play a vital role in our ecosystems and the economy as well, because they contribute to pest control. They continue to seed dispersal and also pollination of some important fruits. So we need to conserve their habitats so that they can continue providing those services to us.
There are plans to expand the programme across the country, and to translate the material into other languages.
We're aiming to change people's attitudes so that whenever there is a potential future outbreak, it might be curbed because people will know how to act responsibly.

LINK: But the risk doesn’t come only from our brushes with wild animal populations. There’s danger much closer to home: in the way we rear and produce our food.

UPSOUND: Philip Lymbery: The health of humans is interrelated with the health of animals, which is interrelated with the ecosystem.

VO: Philip Lymbery is the CEO of Compassion in World Farming, which campaigns for an end to factory farming. When domestic animals come into contact with wildlife, they encounter new pathogens that spread rapidly through a crowded farm.

UPSOUND: Philip Lymbery: A bit like kids in a classroom. Too many animals in too small a space provides the perfect conduit for disease to pass through the flock or the herd. And as it does so, the virus can mutate and rise in its pathogenicity. Its dangerousness.

UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: And also many of them are clones, they've been bred to grow, they haven't been bred to be disease resistant.

LINK: It may have felt like the pandemic was a welcome distraction from the climate crisis. But the bad news is the drivers of climate change and biodiversity loss are also the drivers of pandemics. The COVID-19 pandemic and the ones to follow are all about the way we live on this planet.

VO: That’s why we need scientists like Markotter and her team to explore bat caves and the diseases they hold: it’s the first step away from reacting to new pathogens as they emerge, and towards preventing spillovers from happening in the first place.

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: All predictions are, if we keep on doing things the way we do it, the way we live with animals and the environment, we're going to see more pandemics. We really need to look at a more holistic picture going forward.


PROMO 1 (21 SEC)

UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: Seventy percent of emerging diseases are linked to a zoonoses spillover, so it came from an animal
VO: COVID-19 has turned our world upside down, but have we learned enough to prevent this from happening again?
UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: This isn't the first and it won't be the last.
UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We really need to look at a more holistic picture, going forward.


PROMO 2 (21 SEC)
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Before this, my only association with bats was Batman. But now look at me
VO: What does scrambling around in a sinkhole have to do with preventing the next global pandemic? Take the plunge with us to find out!
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Watch it fly away. Ok, cute but not so cute!


TEASER (11 SEC)
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: There’s no denying it: bats have a bad reputation, but these little guys might help us prevent the next pandemic.

For decades, scientists have predicted a highly contagious pandemic would one day ravage the world’s population and crash global financial markets. They didn’t know how it would start, but they knew to follow the clues. Then the COVID-19 pandemic finally proved them right. Now, South African researchers are heading into bat caves in search of crucial scientific data that could help prevent the next pandemic. Script: CLAIRE TIKTOK VIDEOS: Nurse: Well done. What a well-behaved lady! Claire: They gave me a lollipop! LINK: Over a year ago, I was subjected to a very painful series of injections, all in the name of storytelling. Thanks to the pandemic, it’s taken some time to get here, but I’m about to meet a population of bats. VO: I have a team of researchers patiently waiting to do the introductions. The colony roosts in a deep sinkhole. Dr Low de Vries gives me a quick rundown on what to expect… UPSOUND: Low de Vries: Once you get inside it’s a bit small, so just watch your head… Claire: Say nice things, Low. Say nice things… UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We choose specific sites where we think there's a risk of transmission in terms of the environment, livestock sometimes in the areas, or people. This specific site, we chose because it's in an urban area, so it's close to cities. VO: For over a decade, Professor Wanda Markotter has tested bats for zoonotic pathogens: that is, diseases that commonly occur in animals, but may “spill over” into human beings. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We’re virologists, which means we're looking for viruses, but to get to the virus part, we need the samples. We go down, we catch the bats and we get the samples. And then we go into the lab where we identify the viruses. VO: The first team has just emerged with a handful of bats – carefully transported in fabric bags. These are long-fingered bats, known to carry zoonotic diseases - which is why the researchers wear protective gear to handle them. LINK: Sixty percent of human diseases come from animals, and 75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic. Some more familiar names: smallpox, ebola. HIV, and COVID-19. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: Unfortunately, the species that we identify the most viruses in are bats. They have large diversity, there's more than 1400 species. So that's one of the reasons why we're identifying a lot of viruses in them: there's a lot of bats. VO: Besides taking blood, saliva and faecal samples for analysis in the lab, the scientists also tattoo each bat with a unique number so they can track individuals over time. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: And we're also looking at human behaviour. We're looking at the environment - if people have contact with the bats in this area. And then all that data are made available to the governmental departments so that they can do risk assessments. VO: This batch of bats is returning to the cave, which means it’s time for me to suit up! UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: It’s about to get real, friends… VO: This is serious PPE: overalls, a double layer of gloves and rubber boots. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Research chic! VO: This space-age helmet with built-in respirator ensures that I won’t inhale the air inside the cave. Although the viruses lurking there may not be identical to those that infect humans, it’s vital that we don’t give them a chance to jump hosts. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: I’m ready, guys. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: It's all about adaptation. So if you look at the bat viruses, very few of them have the correct protein to bind to a human cell. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Wish me luck! UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: But let's say I go into this cave every day and I go and crawl around...You give those viruses the opportunity to see human cells every day, they start evolving. And the virus are going to change, to infect the new host. UPSOUND: Camerawoman: What did he say? Claire Mawisa: There's a rung missing at the bottom of the very rusty ladder! VO: Unfazed by the flustered bats, our scientists get to work. Urine and faeces often harbour pathogens and are an easy route for disease transmission. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We take one swab to take a bit of faecal, we put it in a tube and that goes to the lab… LINK: The proximity of this bat population to the urban human population is a big part of the problem. Rubbing shoulders with wildlife in habitats that used to be theirs means we’re not only sharing their space: we might also start sharing their diseases. UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: Undoubtedly there is an increase in these spillover events. It's - there are many drivers. Most of them are what we call anthropogenic, which means they're based on humans. More and more we are putting pressure on wildlife and their habitats, including eating them, selling them, moving them around, keeping them as pets. VO: Professor Delia Randolph is an epidemiologist whose research focuses on the role of food in novel disease outbreaks, especially the food sold in informal markets. UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: You will see wild meat along with domestic meat, along live animals along with dead animals all mixed up. Food, which might be maybe even condemned in one place, gets diverted and sold in another place. So these foods are an opportunity of bringing people into contact with new diseases. UPSOUND: Low de Vries: What we always do is we look for a tattoo number. So then we know she’s a recapture. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: This is gonna go for processing and come back. VO: With that, visiting time is over… UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: I have so much respect for the scientists who do this work, but it’s time for me to get out of here! VO: …and what goes down, must go up again. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Ah, not again! LINK: In 2018, the WHO added an unknown Disease X to its list of priority diseases for which to develop vaccines and treatments. Disease X would have a mortality rate higher than that of the seasonal flu but would spread as easily as the flu. It would shake financial markets before it reached pandemic status. Sound familiar? UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: Epidemiologists have been saying for decades there is going to be a big human pandemic, which is going to kill millions of people and cost trillions of dollars but no one believed us. If you pick up these new diseases just as they're spilling over, you can save more than 90 percent of the costs. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: You have to think differently after this pandemic. If I'm just going into a cave testing for pathogens, what difference are that going to make? UPSOUND: Tedson Nkoana: We interact a lot with the kids because kids act as amplifiers of knowledge. VO: This is where Markotter’s colleague Tedson Nkoana comes in, running community education sessions as part of a United Nations initiative to help curb the impact of COVID-19. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: what is the response? Do they get it? Tedson Nkoana: I have to say I've gotten quite a positive response from the areas that we worked on, and people are now beginning to grasp the idea that there's these bats that might be carrying these diseases and we don't have to be scared of them. VO: The sessions emphasise the risk of contact with points of disease transmission like urine or saliva. But Nkoana also seeks to change the narrative about bats. UPSOUND: Tedson Nkoana: Bats play a vital role in our ecosystems and the economy as well, because they contribute to pest control. They continue to seed dispersal and also pollination of some important fruits. So we need to conserve their habitats so that they can continue providing those services to us. There are plans to expand the programme across the country, and to translate the material into other languages. We're aiming to change people's attitudes so that whenever there is a potential future outbreak, it might be curbed because people will know how to act responsibly. LINK: But the risk doesn’t come only from our brushes with wild animal populations. There’s danger much closer to home: in the way we rear and produce our food. UPSOUND: Philip Lymbery: The health of humans is interrelated with the health of animals, which is interrelated with the ecosystem. VO: Philip Lymbery is the CEO of Compassion in World Farming, which campaigns for an end to factory farming. When domestic animals come into contact with wildlife, they encounter new pathogens that spread rapidly through a crowded farm. UPSOUND: Philip Lymbery: A bit like kids in a classroom. Too many animals in too small a space provides the perfect conduit for disease to pass through the flock or the herd. And as it does so, the virus can mutate and rise in its pathogenicity. Its dangerousness. UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: And also many of them are clones, they've been bred to grow, they haven't been bred to be disease resistant. LINK: It may have felt like the pandemic was a welcome distraction from the climate crisis. But the bad news is the drivers of climate change and biodiversity loss are also the drivers of pandemics. The COVID-19 pandemic and the ones to follow are all about the way we live on this planet. VO: That’s why we need scientists like Markotter and her team to explore bat caves and the diseases they hold: it’s the first step away from reacting to new pathogens as they emerge, and towards preventing spillovers from happening in the first place. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: All predictions are, if we keep on doing things the way we do it, the way we live with animals and the environment, we're going to see more pandemics. We really need to look at a more holistic picture going forward. PROMO 1 (21 SEC) UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: Seventy percent of emerging diseases are linked to a zoonoses spillover, so it came from an animal VO: COVID-19 has turned our world upside down, but have we learned enough to prevent this from happening again? UPSOUND: Delia Randolph: This isn't the first and it won't be the last. UPSOUND: Wanda Markotter: We really need to look at a more holistic picture, going forward. PROMO 2 (21 SEC) UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Before this, my only association with bats was Batman. But now look at me VO: What does scrambling around in a sinkhole have to do with preventing the next global pandemic? Take the plunge with us to find out! UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Watch it fly away. Ok, cute but not so cute! TEASER (11 SEC) UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: There’s no denying it: bats have a bad reputation, but these little guys might help us prevent the next pandemic.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Most of us didn't see the COVID-19 pandemic coming. But scientists worldwide researching diseases with pandemic potential warn that this is not the last or the worst pandemic coming our way.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the middle of the worst pandemic in a century, we speak to the scientists for whom pathogens like SARS-CoV-2 are bread and butter. We will visit Africa's only biosafety level 4 laboratory, at the NICD and get unique access to a cave in Limpopo where scientists from UP are monitoring infectious diseases circulating in local bat populations. We ask: What do we know about emerging infectious diseases? How do we identify unknown threats? What are the driving factors of the increase in zoonotic spill-over events? How can we prevent another COVID-19?
metadata.Summary: In 2018 the WHO added Disease X to its list of priority diseases for which to develop vaccines and treatments. Disease X would “have a mortality rate higher than a season flu but [one that] would spread as easily as the flu…. It would shake financial markets even before it achieved pandemic status.” Sound familiar? The last few decades have seen an acceleration in outbreaks of known and new diseases. Zoonotic infections (diseases that 'spill over' from animals to humans) and especially viruses have been identified as a growing threat. 60% of human diseases come from animals and 75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic. There is a 'spill-over' event 1-2 times per year: an increase of 2-3 times what it was 40 years ago. Around the world, virologists have been raising the red flag about the ways in which our overpopulated, environmentally compromised
metadata.Further information: ZOONOTIC INFECTIONS Zoonotic infectious diseases cause 2.5 billion illnesses and 2.7 million deaths/year. It’s estimated that there are 500 thousand unknown viruses with zoonotic potential. One project found more than 50 SARS-related viruses in bats. It could be so much worse than coronavirus – think about HIV which has killed 65 million people and doesn’t have a cure or a vaccine. Think about SARS with a 10% fatality rate. Or H7N9 with a 40% fatality rate. Or Ebola with 50%. It takes three steps for a zoonotic agent to become pandemic: 1. a human must be exposed to the virus. 2. the virus must either be virulent or become so through mutation. 3. the virus must be able to move from human to human and not kill its host so quickly that it doesn't have time to spread. Each presents opportunities to intervene, but traditionally, the study of infectious disease has focused on containing and tracing outbreaks after they’ve started. CONTRIBUTING FACTORS: Overpopulation Travel and globalisation Encroachment into wild habitats by humans and our farms. Climate change - Biodiversity loss: less dilution, more host-sharing. - Increased interaction between species and with humans. - Increased tick and mosquito-borne diseases. - Shifting habitats, imbalances Increased demand for animal food products (increased NCDs) Bush meat trade (3.4 million tonnes in Africa every year alone) Intensive agricultural practices, especially animal farming - Genetically similar breeds in cramped, stressful, unsanitary conditions - Humans increase contact between different animal species. Domestic animals share highest number of viruses with humans - Land use change is the biggest predictor. - Waste management and anti-microbial resistance: Incubating more virulent and drug resistant strains in domestic animals; 70% of antibiotics are used in farming. - Livestock is 60% of mammal biomass (wildlife 4%). Poultry 70% of bird biomass. Raise and kill 75 billion animals/year. Pandemic is going to worsen AMR: antibiotic prescription, sanitizers. Strategies: - Early detection, early response. Rapid diagnostics - Universal vaccines and drugs - Surveillance at the contact edge - Food/agricultural and environmental interventions. The cost of COVID is around $5-15 trillion versus $22 billion to reduce deforestation and wildlife trafficking CHALLENGES: Wartime budgets are seen as unnecessary in peacetime. The US has reduced funding to programmes for emerging disease research under Trump. Fragmentation of global networks and growing populism threaten bodies like the WHO (it was the UN that funded and organised the drive to eradicate the only disease we have ever actually conquered: smallpox) Science to policy is a big leap. No coordinated response/uniform policy even within the US or EU.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: 1. Travel to Limpopo for two nights to film UP scientists at work monitoring bat populations. They will accommodate us in tents and have said they will cover the costs of our food and PPE 2. Vaccinations for all crew: tetanus and rabies. Tetanus is a once-off; rabies requires two doses 7 days apart. The second dose must be 28 days before the trip. Total cost approx R3 936.84 3. Extra shoot day with internal camera to film at the lab and interview NICD scientists in Joburg
